name: Infrastructure Cost
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Pricing Out a Quantum Computer, Piece by Piece
lesson.summary: Adding up the refrigerator, wiring, control electronics, facility, and staffing behind a current quantum computer already runs into the tens of millions of dollars for a machine with only hundreds of qubits, long before reaching fault tolerance.
lesson.body:
Add up everything covered so far in this chapter, the dilution refrigerator itself, the wiring and control electronics running into and out of it, and the continuous power needed to keep the whole system cold, and a clearer picture emerges of what it actually costs to operate a serious quantum computing research system today. Beyond the refrigerator and its electronics, a real installation also needs a controlled facility environment: vibration isolation so mechanical noise does not couple into the qubits, magnetic shielding to block stray fields that can disturb sensitive quantum states, backup and redundant cooling systems since even a brief warming event can damage or disrupt an experiment in progress, and specialized staff who understand cryogenics, microwave engineering, and quantum control well enough to keep the system running and diagnose problems when something goes wrong.

Room-temperature control electronics add up on a per-qubit basis in a way that is easy to underestimate. Each qubit typically needs its own precisely calibrated combination of signal generation, amplification, and readout hardware, and the cost of these individual channels, while it has been falling as the industry matures, still runs into real money multiplied across every qubit in a system. A complete system, fridge, control racks, and supporting facility, for a current-generation research or early-commercial quantum computer commonly runs into the tens of millions of dollars, and that is for machines holding hundreds to low thousands of physical qubits, nowhere near the million-qubit scale discussed earlier in this chapter.

Extrapolating today's per-qubit costs directly up to a million-qubit machine, without any breakthroughs in the underlying cost structure, would put a fault-tolerant quantum computer at a price tag that is difficult to justify against almost any application, however valuable the answer it produces. This is not a novel situation in the history of computing. Classical computing only became broadly useful once the cost per transistor collapsed by many orders of magnitude, through decades of manufacturing process improvements, not because a hundred-thousand-dollar transistor was ever purchased a billion times over. Quantum computing very likely needs an analogous collapse in the cost of producing, wiring, cooling, and controlling each additional qubit, rather than simply more funding to build the same kind of system bigger.

This is why infrastructure cost is treated as a first-class engineering barrier here rather than a secondary business concern. It is not separable from the physics and engineering challenges already discussed, cryogenics, wiring, and energy; it is essentially those challenges converted into a dollar figure, and it is the number that ultimately decides whether a proposed scaling path is realistic or merely theoretically possible.
